body.text: Tesla and Samsung are among the U.S. firms that have expressed opposition to new tariffs on Vietnam, as an ongoing trade investigation into intellectual property enters its final weeks.

In May, the Trump administration launched an investigation into possible intellectual property violations under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act, announcing that it would examine Vietnam’s “acts, policies, and practices related to IP protection and enforcement and assess their impact on U.S. commerce.” The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) is set to conclude the probe by November 29, at which point it may choose to impose new tariffs on Vietnam.

According to a Reuters report, in July, the EV manufacturer Tesla urged the USTR to “take into account the supply chain needs of American manufacturers” when making its decision on tariffs. It said that “some advanced components and precision manufacturing equipment cannot be sourced domestically despite major investments in U.S. production,” the news agency reported.

The U.S. unit of Samsung, Vietnam’s largest single foreign investor, made a similar argument, Reuters added, noting that Vietnam “produces a significant share of Samsung’s smartphones and network equipment for the U.S. market.”

The hike in tariffs was also opposed by retail groups and trade associations “representing industries with extensive manufacturing operations in Vietnam.” These included makers of footwear, apparel, and other consumer goods.

However, support for tariffs also issued forth from other sectors of U.S. industry, Reuters reported. Industry groups representing American producers of steel, seafood, plywood, solar panels, and wood products “accused Vietnam of unfair practices and called for new tariffs.” Meanwhile, software, film, and music industry groups urged the Trump administration “to secure concrete commitments from Vietnam” aimed at combating IP violations and “widespread piracy.”
In April, USTR Jamieson Greer identified Vietnam as a “priority foreign country” due to its “persistent failure to resolve long-standing concerns about IP protection and enforcement.”

Vietnamese imports are currently subject to a flat 12.5 percent tariff that was imposed in July after a separate Section 301 investigation into the country’s alleged failures to prevent imports of goods made with forced labor – one of 60 nations under review. It is also one of 16 major trading partners that are being subjected to an outstanding investigation into alleged excess manufacturing capacity.

These Section 301 investigations are a way of rescuing President Donald Trump’s protectionist trade policy after the U.S. Supreme Court in February struck down the sweeping “liberation day” tariffs that his administration imposed on allies and adversaries alike last year. Vietnam was hit with one of the highest tariff rates in the world – 46 percent – in recognition of its lopsided trade surplus with the United States. This was later bargained down to 20 percent, before the Supreme Court annulled the tariffs.

The IP and excess manufacturing probes are among the factors that have delayed the conclusion of a final reciprocal trade and tariff agreement between Vietnam and the U.S. Both sides insist that a final deal is close.

After meeting with Vietnamese President To Lam in New York in September, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the two sides had made “substantial progress” and were “very close to reaching the final outcome,” according to Vietnamese media reports. The talks have also been slowed down by U.S. concerns about transshipment – the alleged routing of Chinese goods through Vietnam to avoid U.S. tariffs – and market access for American companies.
